title: Detailed methods and checks of the results

sections.heading: S1. Study scope and data construction
paragraphs: This study uses fictional registries that explicitly list objects, their properties and their names. It does not include the earlier country-fact experiments or four-world pilots. The generator fixed 32 development worlds and 64 worlds reserved for confirmation; both stages have now been evaluated. Files named REGISTRATION record the inputs and code fixed before each local run, linked by file hashes. Development registrations were internal, not public preregistration. The six-world diagnosis was planned after the development validation failed and remains exploratory. A new, narrower confirmation plan and code were publicly fixed before the first model calculation on the 64 reserved worlds, as described in S8.

Each world contains four permanent object IDs, four different values for each of color, shape and home, and four statements assigning aliases to objects. Two aliases name the same object; another names a distractor, and a fourth supplies context. A nameplate is a label, not a permanent ID. The eight selected alias words were apple, bat, anchor, date, cat, basket, fig and dog. We chose them using only how both models' tokenizers divide the prompts into tokens, without looking at model answers. Individual words appear in more than one world, but the complete ordered assignments of values to objects do not repeat.

Each world supplies 96 prompts: two orders of the equivalent names, four Focus conditions, and twelve questions per context. The twelve questions comprise nine factual questions about three aliases, two identity questions, and one registry-status question. Focus is a prompt highlight: it is absent, names either equivalent alias, or names an unrelated alias. Swapping the equivalent names between their binding lines does not change which object either name refers to. Across worlds, we balance the target record's position, alias-line positions, object IDs, the roles assigned to names, and two wording formats. This balance does not cover every possible combination of factors. Both models receive the same 32 development worlds, with 3,072 prompts each, and the same 64 confirmation worlds, with 6,144 prompts each. The two models do not double the number of worlds. Balancing and unique complete field assignments also couple the generated worlds; the independent-world assumption used for intervals is a reference approximation.

sections.heading: S2. Fixed model versions, execution and answer grading
paragraphs: Each model uses its fixed tokenizer and chat template. We use eager attention, process one prompt at a time, use float32 arithmetic, disable TensorFloat-32, and use one CPU thread. At each step, we retain the model's original, or native, output scores for its entire token vocabulary at one output position. Greedy generation chooses the highest-scoring next token. We grade the entire decoded answer after normalizing case, whitespace and final punctuation. We do not remove explanations to turn a response into a correct answer; invalid or extra text remains an error. The intervention runs allow eight new tokens and record whether generation stops on an end-of-sequence token. None of the final diagnostic answers was cut short by the token limit.

rows: Python 3.12.15; PyTorch 2.6.0+cu124; CUDA 12.4; NVIDIA A40 for development and NVIDIA RTX A6000 for confirmation

sections.heading: S3. Search sequence and the six validation cases
paragraphs: The first exploratory search replaced internal outputs at the end-of-alias marker, before the prompt stated the requested field. It tested 35 layer boundaries and then attention heads in two selected layers, using eight development cases. A separate search at the answer position used the same eight cases. In that search, the donor computation already included the requested field. We compared attention to the correct and wrong records across all 36 layers and 32 heads, then selected two candidates. This selection used the correct-answer labels. The later operation transferred the attention shares for all four records without taking answer labels as inputs. With the best candidate, layer 28, head 0 with counting starting at zero, the first token became correct in five of eight cases. This was a promising preliminary result, not a measurement of complete-answer repair.

We then fixed that head and tested the six remaining eligible development worlds. They were separate from the eight search cases, but we had already examined their behavioral answers. A case qualified when the model answered all three fields and the identifier question correctly using the donor alias. With the equivalent recipient alias, it also had to give a completed answer from another listed record for at least one factual question. The recipient questions included eight wrong answers and ten initially correct answers, which we checked for damage. The development diagnosis split the intervention into parts and tested them on these same six worlds, without changing the component or cases. These historical cases remain distinct from the 30 fresh cases selected for the later independent estimate.

sections.heading: S5. Nine fixed interventions and what they change
paragraphs: The nine conditions below belong to the development diagnosis, not the four-condition confirmation. We summarize attention in three ways. Record mass is the sum of attention probabilities on the tokens in one printed object record. The record profile is each record's share of the total attention on all records. The within-record pattern is each token's share of its own record's attention. The four profile/pattern conditions in the table keep the recipient's total attention on records unchanged. The donor and recipient value vectors at record positions must be identical byte for byte. These are the internal vectors that attention combines to form a head's output. We change that output before the attention output projection, the step that mixes head outputs. Calculations use float64 coefficients and float32 contractions, or weighted vector sums. For each field, we hold the change fixed at the original answer-query position throughout answer generation. We do not move it to newly generated positions. For the random control, matching the norm means matching the length of the whole-head change vector.

rows: Use donor color-question record shares; retain recipient within-record patterns and record total.
Use same-field donor record shares; retain recipient patterns and total.
Use same-field donor token patterns; retain recipient record shares and total.
Use both same-field donor factors; retain recipient record total.
Replace the complete attention-weighted contribution of all record tokens, including donor record total.
Replace donor minus recipient remainder after subtracting their record contributions.
Add donor minus recipient natural head output; comparator, not a performance upper bound.
Deterministic random direction matching only the whole-head change's norm, not every factor's dose.

sections.heading: S6. Pre-set success criteria, failed tests and statistical limits
paragraphs: The original validation required at least four of eight errors to be repaired across at least three worlds. It allowed at most one initially correct, protected answer to become wrong. It also required at least two more repairs than a fixed average profile from discovery. Reverse and cyclic interventions each had to produce at least nine of eighteen specified record answers across at least three worlds. Cyclic success also required at least two target IDs. These steering targets were scored separately from factual correctness. The primary profile repaired one error, in world 029. Reverse and cyclic tests each reached one specified target. No intervention passed its full set of success criteria, so this positive-mechanism route did not qualify for confirmation. S8 describes the separate, later plan to estimate the unchanged repair on fresh cases; it does not change these failed results.

The nine-condition development diagnosis generated 162 answers. The seven new conditions, comprising six targeted changes and the random control, each repaired zero of eight errors. Replaying the old profile reproduced its one repair. Every condition preserved the ten initially correct, protected answers. These results did not establish a reliable repair on those development cases; they did not show that the copying rule could never work on fresh cases. The saved scores for the first answer token show that the changes did affect the model. We measured the score of the single token for the prescribed correct answer, called the canonical token, minus the score of the fixed first token of the original wrong response. This margin improved by 6.00 on average for the old profile, 4.05 for the same-field profile, and 4.21 for whole-head transfer. These describe score changes, not complete-answer accuracy or probability sums over accepted answer variants.

For the behavioral intervals, we resample whole worlds 2,000 times, keeping each world's repeated questions and conditions together. These describe variation in the development data; they are not confirmation tests and do not treat questions as independent samples. Additional wrong-record intervals use the retrospective seed 20261115. Predictive comparisons keep entire worlds out of fitting when testing on them. Intervals calculated with the saved predictions held fixed do not include uncertainty from refitting or model selection.

sections.heading: S7. Numerical checks and links to the original records
paragraphs: For the development diagnosis, we set a maximum difference of 0.00002 for reconstructing the unmodified head output and for drift at the fixed query position during generation. The observed query drift was zero. Record profiles require total attention mass of at least 0.0001 and attention on each record of at least 0.00000001. Checks of full-head reconstruction, recombination of record and residual parts, and the random change's norm all passed. Thirty-six unmodified forward passes replayed exactly. Eighteen self-control and eighteen old-profile complete-answer trajectories also matched exactly, including their generation steps. The CPU audit recomputed component changes from saved tensors and checked recorded native scores; it did not rerun model inference. A separate grader read the literal prompts and agreed with the answer grades. That development run used 360 native forward passes, meaning actual model calculations. We did not change a failed success criterion, the component or the intervention strength to obtain success.

The stage labels below locate the development records in S1 Data. Each twelve-character digest prefix is only a short guide to a file, not its full identity. S1 Data and the original registration, custody and audit records retain the full original paths, SHA-256 digests and artifact links. They document where the local execution inputs and outputs came from. These development records are not public preregistration and do not, by themselves, constitute a public data deposit. Confirmation uses its separately published protocol and later records described in S8 and S9.

sections.heading: S8. Publicly fixed independent confirmation plan
paragraphs: The 64 reserved worlds had received no model forward passes when we fixed the new confirmation protocol. Before the first such calculation, the protocol and source were published at GitHub tag confirmation-protocol-20261116-v1, commit f1d7836c653a82c0183c8bfed59c2c1153f73e42. This was a separately planned repetition of the naming test and an estimate of the unchanged repair, not confirmation that the earlier failed mechanism candidate had qualified. Earlier internal registrations and failed requirements remain unchanged. The confirmation registration is identified by SHA-256 e45ce4883bdb6af99921018773055f90d683e1baf4c61b2c75338d4bb048bbf3.

Both models received all 6,144 questions from the same 64 fresh worlds: 4,608 factual questions, 1,024 permanent-label questions and 512 status questions per model. There were 1,536 equivalent-name factual pairs per model. Their prompts, tokenizer assets, model versions and full-answer grading were fixed. These are 64 shared worlds, not 128 independent worlds. World facts and base prompts were checked against the original model-free generator. No case or prompt was replaced after an unfavorable answer.

Only Qwen received internal changes. We required a donor alias with all three factual answers and the identity answer strictly correct, and an equivalent recipient alias with at least one finished wrong-object factual answer. The original selection seed, reference-causal-discovery-20261115-v1, fixed the checksum ordering of worlds, eligible contexts and the screening wrong field. We selected one context from every eligible world using only unchanged answers. All initially wrong recipient fields then counted as possible repairs, and all initially correct recipient fields counted as protected answers. The full selected cohort, not a favorable subset, supplied the estimate.

The selected component remained layer 28, head 0, using zero-based indices. Four conditions covered every selected recipient color, shape and home question: exact unchanged replay; the correct donor's color-question record shares; the fixed mean of all eight discovery donor-color profiles; and the recipient's own color-question record shares. The fixed mean, keyed A through D, was [0.17506461211422675, 0.6395382948200473, 0.024789365765038294, 0.16060772730068765]. This eight-world mean differs from the mean of the other seven worlds used in the earlier discovery-ranking comparison. New-world profiles did not update it. No head, strength or copying rule was tuned. Reverse, cyclic, same-field, whole-head and random changes were not part of this confirmation.

The primary change retained recipient value vectors, total record attention, relative token weights within each record and attention outside records. The donor color profile was reused across the three properties, but each recipient question supplied its own first-step additive change. This fixed change stayed at the original question position throughout complete greedy generation. Natural captures had to match their saved baseline scores, record value hashes had to agree across the six unchanged name/property combinations, first-step record-weight and additive outputs had to agree exactly, and zero-change replay had to reproduce complete native trajectories. Query drift could not exceed 0.00002. Unsupported calculations or failed checks would stop the stage, not permit smoothing, new cases or a new component.

The planned primary rate averaged the fraction of initially wrong facts repaired separately within each eligible world, so a world with three errors did not count three times as much as one with one error. Pooled error counts were retained as a separate descriptive measure. We fixed a 50% world-balanced repair target and a 25-percentage-point advantage over the fixed mean profile. These are new estimation targets with a different weighting from the earlier pooled four-of-eight and two-of-eight requirements; they do not redefine those failures. At least 20 eligible worlds were required for a usefulness conclusion. With fewer, the result would be labeled imprecise without replacement worlds or additional search.

For the primary world-balanced rate, the pre-set reference interval added and subtracted sqrt(log(40)/(2n)), where n is the number of eligible worlds, then limited the endpoints to zero and one. This is Hoeffding's bounded-mean interval under the stated independent-world approximation. The paired primary-minus-mean difference used twice that radius and endpoints limited to minus one and one. The 50% target would be excluded only if the primary upper endpoint was below 50%, and supported for repair benefit alone only if the lower endpoint reached 50%; otherwise it remained uncertain. Benefit alone did not establish a useful overall fix.

Confirmation behavioral uncertainty used 2,000 whole-world bootstrap resamples with seed 20261116. Affected-world prevalence also received two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson binomial reference intervals. Preservation used an exact one-sided 95% binomial-reference upper bound on the fraction of worlds with any damaged protected answer, counting only worlds containing at least one such answer. We reported whether this upper bound was below 10%, rather than assuming zero risk from no observed damage. These intervals use an independent, identically distributed world approximation for the artificial generator; balancing and unique full fact assignments limit that approximation. They are individual reference intervals, not simultaneous confidence for both models, all comparisons or combined benefit and safety. Fixed-sample counts remain exact descriptive results.

sections.heading: S9. Confirmation results, checks and later descriptive breakdowns
paragraphs: Qwen answered 3,656 of 4,608 fresh factual questions correctly, made 952 wrong-object factual errors and no other factual errors, and showed 265 strict correct-versus-wrong-object disagreements among 1,536 equivalent-name pairs. These disagreements affected 48 of 64 worlds; wrong-object errors of any kind affected 59 worlds. Phi answered 3,782 factual questions correctly, made 546 wrong-object and 280 other factual errors, and showed 166 strict pair disagreements across 38 worlds; wrong-object errors of any kind affected 53 worlds. Strict object-label answers were correct in 699 of 1,024 Qwen questions and 50 of 1,024 Phi questions. Both models answered all 512 status questions correctly. These strict identifier scores were not replaced by a new permissive formatting analysis.

Thirty fresh Qwen worlds met the unchanged eligibility rule. Their 90 recipient facts included 40 initial errors and 50 protected correct answers. The four conditions generated 360 complete answers and 720 greedy-generation steps; every answer finished in two tokens including its end marker. The correct-donor profile repaired 16 errors in 15 worlds and damaged no protected fact. The fixed mean repaired seven errors in seven worlds without damage. The recipient-color profile repaired six errors in six worlds and damaged one protected home answer. Unchanged replay repaired none and preserved the entire baseline trajectory. Two worlds had all three recipient facts initially wrong; only 28 worlds contributed protected facts.

The primary world-balanced repair fraction was 41.6667%, with the planned reference interval 16.8712% to 66.4621%. Its pooled rate was 16/40, or 40%. The fixed mean had a world-balanced rate of 17.7778% and the recipient-color profile 20.0000%. The paired primary-minus-mean advantage was 23.8889 percentage points, with the planned interval -25.7020 to 73.4797 points. The observed primary rate and advantage were below their 50% and 25-point targets, and the intervals did not establish or rule out the primary repair target. The saved conclusion was uncertain, not a passed candidate or an excluded useful effect.

Zero damaged worlds among the 28 with protected facts gave a one-sided 95% damage-risk upper reference bound of 10.1466%, rounded to 10.15% in the main text. This does not establish risk below 10%. The recipient-color comparison damaged one of those worlds, with an upper bound of 15.8507%. Protected fact counts and affected-world risk answer different questions; neither is a guarantee for unrelated tasks. The overall assessment did not claim simultaneous confidence that the repair was useful, superior and safe.

The table below is a later descriptive breakdown, not a new pre-set success test. It lists all three properties rather than selecting the most favorable one. There were 18 protected color facts, 18 protected shape facts and 14 protected home facts. Primary and mean-profile changes damaged none; the recipient-color change damaged one home fact. The primary correction therefore sometimes transferred beyond the color source question, but this is not proof of a property-independent or abstract entity signal.

The eligible target IDs were A in ten worlds, B in ten, C in five and D in five. Primary repairs occurred in four A worlds, three B worlds, four C worlds and four D worlds. The corresponding error counts repaired were 4/15 for A, 3/12 for B, 4/5 for C and 5/8 for D. These selected subgroups are small and unbalanced; the differences are not independent tests of which ID is easier. Across all 40 initial errors, seven were repaired by both the primary and fixed mean, nine by the primary only, none by the mean only, and 24 by neither. Each property contributed three primary-only repairs. These post-result summaries do not replace the pre-set targets or their uncertainty calculations.

The fixed native audits passed for all 6,144 Qwen answers, all 6,144 Phi answers and the complete 360-answer repair grid. They checked saved full-vocabulary greedy choices and decoding, native unchanged replays, recipient record-weight arithmetic, fixed query positions and deltas, and source/custody bindings. The separately written literal-prompt grader independently matched complete behavioral coverage, correct answers, all selected cases and repair counts. Separate read-only reconstruction also matched the reported statistical ranges. These checks used saved values, not new model inference. Confirmation used an NVIDIA RTX A6000, whereas development used an A40; the study did not isolate hardware effects on differences between stages.

The confirmation native-repair receipt is identified by SHA-256 be92e50954d30c8151a8d564e96ec4639fbcb12bfbbb2cae5ef34e24f80402eb, and the independent literal receipt by 32f6c8e29003d108054aec12b986a590dfff3339b5b9efb82f5f2b44c79fb785. Full stage inputs, per-case answers, checksums and custody links accompany the released records. A passed audit establishes fidelity of execution and recorded outcomes; it does not promote the failed original mechanism gate, remove sampling uncertainty, or establish that entity representations are absent.
